t: LeetCode 2128 - Remove All Ones With Row and Column Flips: A Rank-One XOR Certificate
o: **Understanding the problem.** A move flips every bit of one chosen row or column, and we ask whether some sequence of moves erases all 1s. Flips commute and applying the same flip twice cancels, so without loss of generality each of the m + n lines is flipped zero or one times. Example 1 succeeds: flipping the middle row makes it match the outer rows' pattern, and flipping the middle column then zeroes the board. Example 2 fails because the lone 1 at the top-right can never be isolated - any flip touching its cell drags a partner along. Example 3 already has no 1s. Since m and n reach 300, enumerating the 2^(m+n) flip combinations is hopeless; we need a structural certificate checkable in O(mn).
k: Row/column flips commute and are self-inverse, so assume each line is flipped at most once.
After any sequence, cell (i,j) equals original XOR rowFlip[i] XOR colFlip[j]; zeroing everything forces exactly this XOR structure.
Consequently every row must equal the first row or its bitwise complement.
Both views reduce to one identity: grid[i][j] ^ grid[0][j] ^ grid[i][0] ^ grid[0][0] must be 0 everywhere.

a.i: Fix the first row as the reference pattern. Column flips act on all rows identically and row flips toggle whole rows, so clearing the board is possible iff every other row equals the first row or its complement. If that holds, flipping the columns where the first row has a 1, then flipping any all-one rows, gives an explicit solution.
s: For each subsequent row, compute flip = row[0] ^ row0[0], deciding whether this row should match row0 or its complement.
Verify every entry satisfies row[j] == row0[j] ^ flip; fail otherwise.
Return true if all rows pass - a concrete flip sequence exists by construction.
a.t: O(m*n) - each cell is compared against the first-row pattern once

a.i: Model flips as XOR masks r_i and c_j: after all moves, cell (i,j) shows g_ij ^ r_i ^ c_j. Requiring zeros everywhere means g_ij must equal r_i ^ c_j, so g_ij ^ g_0j ^ g_i0 ^ g_00 collapses to (r_i^c_j)^(r_0^c_j)^(r_i^c_0)^(r_0^c_0) = 0 automatically. Conversely, if the identity holds, choosing r_i = g_i0 and c_j = g_0j ^ g_00 clears the board - necessity and sufficiency in one expression.
s: Anchor on the corner value g00 = grid[0][0].
For every cell (i, j), evaluate grid[i][j] ^ grid[0][j] ^ grid[i][0] ^ g00.
Return false at the first nonzero result.
Return true if no violation exists.
a.t: O(m*n) - constant XOR work per cell, early exit on first violation

w: In an interview, derive the commutativity/self-inverse facts aloud, then either normalize against the first row or present the XOR identity and code the O(mn) check. Pitfalls: trying BFS over board states (the space is exponential), accepting only exact matches with row0 while forgetting complements, and assuming flip order matters. Edge cases: an all-zero grid, [[0]], and single-row or single-column matrices (always clearable). Natural follow-up: the minimum number of flips to clear the grid, which falls out greedily from the same normalization.
